Things I like
- Story is gripping, twists are fun although some are quite predictable
- Atmosphere is strong, with the right feelings of paranoia and eerieness.
- Simple controls but with a lot to do
- Character list kept short, but with a lot of personality
- Choices matter

Things I dislike:
- Jumpscares. They're not needed, wanted, or help anything or anyone. They just come up randomly for a cheap shock.
- The endings are either far too vague to properly understand, or too deep to easily understand. I can't tell which, but I didn't get as much from it as I hoped.
- If you accidentally mis-click a dialogue option, or you do something else dumb, there's a good chance you're gonna need to restart the entire game to rectify it. This is also true of endings, so you'd better be prepared to replay the game at least 3 times.

[h1][b] TLDR: While not noteworthy in any direction, it’s a decent low-budget mystery/thriller that is acceptable for its price. [/b] [/h1]

[h1]PROS: [/h1]
➕Good concept with phone imitation and believable features
➕Multiple decision-based endings


[h1]CONS: [/h1]
➖Severe lack of options, not even fullscreen toggle or audio options??
➖Missing some essential phone features, like ease of scrolling through tons of text messages or jumping to specific times in videos
➖Some cringe voice acting/FMV

[h1] [b] Content (Game world/Narrative) – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
The game world takes place entirely on a phone, using the phone's UI screen. It’s a very simple imitation, but most of it works as you’d expect a phone to function. You have various apps that you go through, including email, messaging, Twitter-like  social media, photos, and dating apps. As far as a phone imitation goes, I’d say the world is fairly good, though it is missing some obvious features like being able to click on a point-in-time on a video to move to that section, or scrolling through hundreds of text messages. Otherwise, it’s good. 

The narrative focuses on a girl named Anna, who has seemingly disappeared. For some reason, Anna’s phone ends up in your possession and you have to sleuth around to figure out what happened and how to find her. 
The story has branching paths that ultimately comes down to which person you end up believing and siding with, as well as specific choices along the way that influence the ending of the game. 
I got the “Worst” ending, but was still satisfied with my playthrough because I did everything sensible and logical that I would do. To achieve the better endings, you have to do questionably moral things like [spoiler]siding with a sex offender when you have limited information[/spoiler], or [spoiler]confessing love to Anna’s best friend while pretending to be Anna.[/spoiler] In a way, it's sleazy and morally ambiguous, but I do also understand the phishing aspect of it and needing to obtain information any way possible. 
In the end, I found the story to be only “Ok” . The antagonist of a [spoiler]rogue AI[/spoiler] wasn’t very exciting or scary at the end. 

[h1][b] Gameplay (Mechanics/Difficulty) – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
The general gameplay loop is to explore around the phone UI solving puzzles to advance the plot. 
The mechanics remind me of a watered-down version of The Rootrees Are Dead (great game, check out my review [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/Synikx/recommended/2754380?snr=1_5_9__402]here[/url]), how you have to use hints to sleuth around a phone for information. I’d say about 70% of the puzzles in the game consist of either decoding messages or pictures, whereas the other 30% is about researching information. 
The picture/message decoding consists of either aligning pictures correctly, or putting text messages in the correct order. I found the picture puzzles to be much more challenging. The researching of information is where it’s similar to Rootrees where you need to look through emails or messages to find correct information for things like passwords. 
While the mechanics were fine, I would have much preferred the quantity of research to picture/text decoding to be reversed, that is 70% research and 30% decode. I felt like the decoding was a bit out of place. 

The difficulty is generally easy. I was stumped a few times, but the game allows a skip or nudges you in the right direction after a little bit. The only challenging part is figuring out the very specific choices to get the better endings. 

[h1] [b] Technical (Graphics/Performance) – [5/10] [/b] [/h1]
Graphics were okay. Most of the game is a phone UI, with the remaining parts being FMV or pictures. I felt that the UI looks simple, but believable. The FMV and pictures were high quality and numerous, especially in public settings, so I appreciated the realistic approach. I’d say this is around PS4-era graphics. 
Performance was flawless, zero issues. 
I do want to call out the atrocious graphical settings. I don’t think I’ve ever seen a game with less options. I think the only two are language and subtitles. Not even audio volume or full screen or resolution. 
I didn’t notice any bugs. 

1440p @ 240hz | installed on SSD  

[h1] [b] Audio – [4/10] [/b] [/h1]
There wasn’t much, if any music. 
There is ample voice acting, and half of it was super cringe. Anna did a decent job. Greg was just terrible. Taylor has ups and downs. Ashley is decent as well. 

[h1] [b] Replay Factor (Longevity) – [4/10] [/b] [/h1]
Decent replay value due to the multiple endings, but you probably need a guide for the route on how to get there. Otherwise, just achievements and easter eggs. 

[h1] [b] Final Verdict – [5/10] [/b] [/h1]
Simulacra is a horror game that takes place entirely on a phone screen, with you being the user operating the phone. This isn’t an overly terrifying game, though there is a few jump scares, and I found the plot to be okay, which is generally the linchpin with these more “Visual novel”-type games with less gameplay depth, so all things considered, it’s a fairly good game, especially for the price. 

I don’t have too many big issues with the game, just smaller ones. 
The graphical options are terrible, but thankfully, I was able to use alt+enter to play in windowed mode, since there’s no borderless option. 
I’d have liked better phone functionality, namely being able to click to any point in time for videos and ease of scrolling through dozens of text messages. Everyone has been using smartphones for decades at this point, so these basic features should be available. 
Lastly, the voice acting was pretty cringy. Cringe was generally the norm, with average performances being the exception. 

Otherwise, the gameplay through small puzzles and sleuthing, and the story, while not exceptional, were both enough to keep me interested until I hit the credits. 
There’s a lot of things that could be improved, but for the price, I think it’s a solid game worth checking out. 

[h1] [b] Recommend? (Price) [Y/N] [/b] [/h1]
[h1]Yes[/h1]
$5 is an acceptable price considering it takes around ~4 hours to beat for a single playthrough and offers multiple endings. Sale price of $1 is very good. 

You can find my curator page here: https://steamcommunity.com/groups/Synik_GR

[h2] Simulacra Review: A Promising Start That Loses Its Way [/h2]

Simulacra is an intriguing, story-driven game that draws players in with its early mystery and atmosphere. However, as the game progresses, it begins to lose momentum, culminating in an abrupt and unsatisfying ending. Despite this, the game is still worth experiencing for those who enjoy narrative-focused titles, though it has a few notable shortcomings.

[h3] The Good: [/h3]

1) Compelling Start: From the beginning, Simulacra presents an engaging and mysterious premise that immediately captures the player's attention. The game’s atmosphere and pacing set the stage for an intriguing narrative.

2) Satisfying Puzzle Solving: For those with a keen eye for detail, solving the puzzles is rewarding. The game often challenges players to analyze small clues, and the sense of satisfaction upon uncovering key pieces of the story is one of its standout features.

3) Impactful Choices: The game does well in giving players the feeling that their choices matter. How you respond to certain characters affects their relationships with you, adding a layer of depth and emotional investment to the experience.

[h3] The Bad: [/h3]

1) Repetitive Gameplay: Unfortunately, the gameplay starts to feel repetitive as the game progresses. The entire experience is confined to a phone screen, and while this fits the premise, it can become tiresome over time, as the game rarely deviates from this formula.

2) Lack of Explanation for the Antagonist: The game’s main antagonist remains cryptic, with little explanation given for their motivations or origins. This leaves players with more questions than answers, which can feel frustrating for those who prefer a clear narrative.

3) Abrupt Ending: One of the biggest letdowns is the ending. For a story-based game, the conclusion should feel like a natural payoff, but instead, it feels rushed and unfinished, leaving many of the game’s intriguing threads unresolved. The game’s narrative feels carried more by its strong start than by its finale.

[h3] The Ugly: [/h3]

1) Repetitive Playthroughs: Replaying the game is a tedious process as players must start from scratch. There is no checkpoint system to revisit critical moments or alter the story’s outcome without going through the entire experience again. This makes multiple playthroughs feel like a chore.

2) Frustrating Achievements: Some of the achievements are either too obscure or require an unreasonable amount of time and patience to unlock. This might be off-putting for those who are not inclined to consult a guide or spend excessive hours grinding.

3) Annoying Sound Effects: While the sound design in Simulacra is generally effective, the game occasionally relies on loud, jarring noises in an attempt to startle the player. These moments feel cheap and detract from the otherwise immersive experience, disrupting the atmosphere rather than enhancing it.

[h3] Conclusion: 6/10 [/h3]

Simulacra has a lot to offer in terms of its mystery and narrative, especially for those who enjoy story-driven experiences. However, the lack of a satisfying ending, repetitive gameplay, and the absence of convenience features like a checkpoint system hold it back from being a truly great game. It’s definitely worth checking out if you’re a fan of mystery and story-focused titles, but if you’re sensitive to flashing lights or sudden loud noises, it might be best to approach with caution.

The game starts in forced-fullscreen, with no in-game options to disable or change that. Alt-Enter wouldn't work initially until I actually went into the game code to change it. Allegedly, this key combo worked for other people according to the abysmally poor 'support' I got from their discord (which forcefully installs itself into your discord when you launch the game). The game starts by telling you, "this game is best experienced with a headset on". Okay, great, I intended to play it that way. Then the Kaigan Games logo feces starts up with 200 decibel loud racket, followed by a bunch of industrial noises and screeching they've deemed 'musical'. Thanks, you kntz, are ya paying for the hearing aid I'm going to need after this introduction to your POS software? HOW am I supposed to know to do that BEFORE bleeding from the ears? Like, SURELY at least one person in this entire game studio must have played the game (on a headset, as they recommended), and thought to themselves, "Gee, maybe this is a bit loud." No volume slider in-game, no independent music-voice-sfx sliders so it's ALL or nothin' with the Windows mixer. GREAT choice guys, leave the game's audio quality in the hands of the people that brought us Windows ME, Vista, 8 and 10. *slowclap*

With this kind of quality product, quality control, quality review, quality support, quality content I look forward to the day when I hear your slapdash company has suffered complete economic failure and I can rest easy knowing I won't have to deal with any further blood in my headphones thanks to you bunch of ridiculous hacks. If there is a higher power, may they see fit to grant each of you the slowest and most painful demise available, all set to the absolute DRECK soundtrack of your own miserable game.

Simulacra wasn't an entirely bad experience. I actually had a decent time with most of the game. However, the overall package is important to me with a game. I only played through Mass Effect 3 once because the endings were so off-putting that I did not have any interest in playing through again because the conclusion lowered the quality of the game as a whole for me. Mind you, Simulacra doesn't have two games that came before it to ruin the legacy of or anything, nor is it even a tenth the length of Mass Effect 3, but an unsatisfying conclusion to any heavily story-focused game is often the ruin of many a game that were doing well up until that point.

With Simulacra, you navigate a missing girl's cell phone, using the text messaging, web browser, social media posts, and a dating app to further your investigation into where the girl is, gain a couple of allies to help with said investigation, and ultimately conclude with a villain which I won't spoil the identity of or anything like that. I will say that you should be able to easily understand a great villain when the villain monologues to you about why said villain is doing things, and there should be some logical explanations for the reasoning for the villain's actions, etc. Also, a villain shouldn't just pop out of nowhere, typically. Imagine if you got to the end of a deep storyline, and suddenly an extraterrestrial pops out without proper foreshadowing. It would make for a "good bad movie," but a terrible plot point. Again, I won't say specifics about this villain, but the villain does not seem to have a very logical viewpoint, and the villain pops practically out of nowhere and can do things that the game never explains which are vital to the main storyline.

Finally, there appear to be four different endings. Apparently the game locks you out of certain endings based on certain actions you take at some point in the game. I have no idea what those actions were or when they came up. Worse yet, there is no manual saving in Simulacra. There is ONE autosave file that overwrites every time you complete an objective, meaning to see the other endings, you have to start the game from the beginning again. The text messages pop up faster than before, but the game still takes too long for me to have the patience to play through it again, especially since the gameplay wasn't particularly enjoyable for me. Simulating a real cell phone was a cool premise, but it wasn't "fun" to interact with for me outside of the initial surprises of what the very small cast of characters (and an even smaller cast of *relevant* characters) have to say.

The ending I got was horribly dark and unpleasant, and the other ending that was offered to me was clearly going to be horribly dark and unpleasant as well. Dark endings can be entertaining if the storyline gives a satisfying quality to them that doesn't leave you feeling cheated. In Simulacra, the villain effectively tells you "lulz, you made decisions (that I'm not going to specify which ones or when) which set this stuff up. Now make horrible choice A, or horrible choice B." I stopped caring about the story immediately upon being given these options, and just proceeded to the ending knowing my conclusion was going to suck because I didn't play with a walkthrough and the game doesn't allow saving aside from the regularly-overwriting autosave, so you can't just load back a few minutes to make a different decision and see things play out differently.

Without very clear points of making relevant decisions, and without a manual save you can load, AND without enjoyable dark/"bad" endings, Simulacra left me disappointed in what initially seemed like a game I was going to talk about to others and say great things about it, but walling off endings sneakily and overwriting autosaves without a manual save option ruined the overall package of this game for me. I already regret the time I spent on it and I'm not going to waste any more of my time looking up the other endings online or replaying it. I will forever remember the crap ending choice the game locked me into and look back on Simulacra with disdain and disappointment.

I already own the sequel, Simulacra 2, but I no longer intend to play it because I dislike the first game so much now.

With Simulacra, you navigate a missing girl's cell phone, using the text messaging, web browser, social media posts, and a dating app to further your investigation into where the girl is, gain a couple of allies to help with said investigation, and ultimately conclude with a villain which I won't spoil the identity of or anything like that. I will say that you should be able to easily understand a great villain when the villain monologues to you about why said villain is doing things, and there should be some logical explanations for the reasoning for the villain's actions, etc. Also, a villain shouldn't just pop out of nowhere, typically. Imagine if you got to the end of a deep storyline, and suddenly an extraterrestrial pops out without proper foreshadowing. It would make for a "good bad movie," but a terrible plot point. Again, I won't say specifics about this villain, but the villain does not seem to have a very logical viewpoint, and the villain pops practically out of nowhere and can do things that the game never explains which are vital to the main storyline. Finally, there appear to be four different endings. Apparently the game locks you out of certain endings based on certain actions you take at some point in the game. I have no idea what those actions were or when they came up. Worse yet, there is no manual saving in Simulacra. There is ONE autosave file that overwrites every time you complete an objective, meaning to see the other endings, you have to start the game from the beginning again. The text messages pop up faster than before, but the game still takes too long for me to have the patience to play through it again, especially since the gameplay wasn't particularly enjoyable for me. Simulating a real cell phone was a cool premise, but it wasn't "fun" to interact with for me outside of the initial surprises of what the very small cast of characters (and an even smaller cast of *relevant* characters) have to say. The ending I got was horribly dark and unpleasant, and the other ending that was offered to me was clearly going to be horribly dark and unpleasant as well. Dark endings can be entertaining if the storyline gives a satisfying quality to them that doesn't leave you feeling cheated. In Simulacra, the villain effectively tells you "lulz, you made decisions (that I'm not going to specify which ones or when) which set this stuff up. Now make horrible choice A, or horrible choice B." I stopped caring about the story immediately upon being given these options, and just proceeded to the ending knowing my conclusion was going to suck because I didn't play with a walkthrough and the game doesn't allow saving aside from the regularly-overwriting autosave, so you can't just load back a few minutes to make a different decision and see things play out differently. Without very clear points of making relevant decisions, and without a manual save you can load, AND without enjoyable dark/"bad" endings, Simulacra left me disappointed in what initially seemed like a game I was going to talk about to others and say great things about it, but walling off endings sneakily and overwriting autosaves without a manual save option ruined the overall package of this game for me. I already regret the time I spent on it and I'm not going to waste any more of my time looking up the other endings online or replaying it. I will forever remember the crap ending choice the game locked me into and look back on Simulacra with disdain and disappointment. I already own the sequel, Simulacra 2, but I no longer intend to play it because I dislike the first game so much now.

[h1]Intro[/h1]
You found a lost phone. Inside, you find someone asking for help. [b]SIMULACRA[/b] puts you in the shoe of a stranger who is trying to find the owner of a lost phone. Will you succeed or will you fail?

[b]Pros:[/b]
- 4 endings with slight story branches
- New game plus let you play the game with faster chat speed

[b]Cons:[/b]
- No manual save and extra save slot to make it easier to unlock all endings
- Not suitable for people who have issues with flashing lights

[b]Specs[/b]
Intel Core i5-9300H 2.40GHz, 8GB RAM, NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1650

[h1]Should you buy this game?[/h1]
[b]Yes.[/b]
[i]If you like to read a visual novel that was told through phone and chats, feel free to buy this game at a sale.[/i]

[hr][/hr]
[h1]In-Depth Review[/h1]

[h3]Visuals[/h3]
As a game that is played out on a smartphone, the game does well to simulate the phone-like interface. It has a photo app, a contact book, a chat app - anything that you'll expect from a smartphone. Its functionality is limited tough. There is no option to switch between tabs nor a scroll bar on the right side of the screen to scroll the page faster.

[h3]Story[/h3]
The story is played out from series of chats. Expect a lot of typos and shortened words due to the informal context. This brings forth the characters' personality though, especially since everyone has a unique texting style from each other. Some information can also be retrieved by watching videos and receiving phone calls, although their voice is not expressive enough - it feels dragged out on purpose to make it easier for non-native English speakers to listen to. It does make them easier to hear, but it also kills their expression in the process.

Interface aside, the presentation helps with the storytelling. The glitchy screen and a few jumpscares help to set the mysterious vibe, while the surprising phone calls freak me out sometimes. It got toned down as you play the game, focusing more on the mysterious element. The writing was done well in regards to what's happening and sometimes, you will have several options to choose from. Despite giving the same outcome, the conversation will play out differently based on which option that you choose. However, some sentences are not flowing smoothly after choosing a certain option, giving you the impression that you chose the wrong one.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2466225479 

[h3]The Game[/h3]
[b]Gameplay[/b]
The gameplay is focused on chatting with people and exploring everything that is inside the phone that you used. As I said before, sometimes you will have to choose between several options to proceed. Some of them will affect the endings, some are not. Some old chat and photos will also be encrypted, allowing you to play a minigame to restore their state, which takes form in arranging photos or word. It's quite easy to finish although some words might be difficult to arrange sometimes.

Hints are usually provided whenever you are stuck. You can ask people to figure out what you are supposed to do and they will gladly help you out. However, I got stuck twice with no idea to proceed. Although one is expected since I never do well with puzzles that have vague rules, another feels like they don't give enough hints to solve.

[b]Length and Difficulty[/b]
I finished the game in ~4h, and proceed to replay the game several times to get all achievements. The new game+ helps a lot by providing a faster chat speed, allowing you to finish the game faster. However, you still need to wait for the voice-over near the ending to finish, and they talk very slowly. It was tiring to wait for them to finish talking and playing the game several times to unlock all four endings become not fun anymore. I wish there is an option to fast-forward the game at this point.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2466225684 

[b]Problems[/b]
Although the game has a phone-like interface, some quality of life features are missing, notably the option to switch tabs in the browser (or the option to keep existing tab), and the feature to start a video from a certain timestamp. There were also some occasions when I had to type some forms and I couldn't use the tab button in my keyboard to switch between text boxes. Lastly, there are some flashing lights near the ending - people who have issues with it might want to stay out of the game.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
For a visual novel game, it still can be enjoyed with people who don't like to read a wall of text. You might need to read a lot, but they are mostly in the form of short chats which shouldn't take long to finish. The story picks up an interesting topic that is enhanced with its mysterious vibe, and although the story feels weak at times, it still proves to be an enjoyable read.

If you have ever wondered how ugly it could get in the event that AI were to take over, well, this game depicts one possible reality. 

Enjoyed it overall, but aiming to reach 100% completion left me with mixed feelings.


Simulacra is a modern take on a philosophical idea that originated in an essay called "Simulacra and Simulation" from 1981. It's simple, and yet, if you manage to reach any ending, and the true ending especially, you will likely ask yourself questions about how you approach your existence in our digitalised world.

The game has its flaws, but if you're okay with this format, then you will probably have a good time.


When I played Simulacra for the first time in 2018, I played it, and I enjoyed it a lot. I was impressed by the simplistic yet effective nature of the storytelling that was made relevant due to the then technologically transitional period: everyone learning how to use smartphones for almost anything. I also appreciated how little the game requires of you, safe for the patience to read, comprehend, observe, and stop to think for a moment, making it an easy recommendation for playing after a mentally and physically demanding day.

That was then. But what about now...?


Lately, I had been thinking a lot about the topics of Simulacra, Simulation, Simulacrum, and AI, so I decided to replay the game and complete it because I liked it so much my first time. It took me 2 playthroughs to reach completion. The first one took 4-5 hours, and the second - no more than 2-3. My recommendation if you were to seek completion within the day would be to do it with a guide next to you. Some achievements, especially the hidden one and the true ending, require noticing and doing a number of things, which could take you hours to nail by going back again and again -- which could be enjoyable if you're into that and are okay with spending more time with the game.

And here is a thing you'll wish to keep in mind: to reach 100% completion, you will need to open the corresponding save file folder, and create multiple backups (ideally, giving yourself context because it gets hard to make out the saves), because you will need to go back if you don't want to replay the game 5 or 6 times. Most of all, the save files will help you in the event that the game bugs out, as it tends to do -- for instance, when you use your keyboard to input something, and then press Enter, the game crashes; for others, some chats don't load properly; for others yet, some achievements refuse to pop up on the first or second try; and so on.


Do your due diligence to find out what's needed for 100% completion. I used Naps' guide on PlayStationTrophies.org, and made plenty of back up saves along the way. Feel free to comment if you need the files for your run, though imo it's more fun to do it along the way.

You might think that this is a real-life mystery-horror thriller but no, you will find out that it is a B film in disguise - nonsensical plot, cringy acting, annoying jumpscares, and clichéd ending in one package!

The game was quite intriguing in the beginning. We have to use someone's phone to find out what happened to its owner. To my disappointment, the game got downhill fast.

Puzzles were OK, but watching the video messages was painful. If the devs didn't have enough fundings to hire good actors, then why not just leave out the video? They don't contribute to the plot anyway. There were also jumpscares, which were so out of place and annoying, all sense of immersion I had was ruined by them.

[spoiler]The worst was the ending. The villain was revealed to be an AI called Simulacra, who wanted to kill Anna because, in Simulacra's own words, she "is a worm in a perfect image that needs to be eradicated". Was this line supposed to be scary? Why does Simulacra speak like a cartoon villain?

The ending left me with more questions than answers. The biggest question is: How does an entity that only exists in the virtual space hijack people's bodies in real life?!?!?! Is there a Wi-Fi receiver in the human brain!? 

Even the story premise falls apart when you think about it: 
WHY did the villain/sockpuppet leave the phone on the player's doorstep in the first place?
If Simulacra could imitate other people in the cyberspace, then it could have just destroyed the phone and used Anna's identity to lure more victims online (indeed, at one point in the game Simulacra successfully wiped the phone data), instead of letting the player find out about Anna, who might then rescue her, or worse, warn everyone in the world about the existence of a cyberspace killer. On the topic of warning people, why didn't people who knew Anna contact the police instead of trying to solve the case on their own? When even an ordinary person realised that something fishy was going on, how come the police knew nothing about the disappearances when all the missing people had interacted with each other before they went missing? Did they not bother to do basic investigations?[/spoiler]

Finally, as a VN, being unable to manually save is unacceptable. You have to replay the game from the beginning to get an alternative ending.

It's a shame as this game had great potential to educate people about phone addiction and danger of social media.

Summary: For a horror/mystery/puzzle game, it is quite weak on each of the three elements. The least surprising mystery game I've played. Perhaps mainly because it blows its load from the start and spends the rest of the play time catching up with itself. Probably works better on mobile, as it seems made for a short attention span.

Pros:
- Basic concept is a cool commentary on social media and online dating
- A couple of surprising moments
- Some easter eggs and alternative paths give a bit of replay value

Cons:
- Storytelling is overstated and predictable
- Dialog is unconvincing, and I often didn't like my choices
- Game is linear and holds your hand almost the entire way. Some light puzzles, but otherwise no challenge, except unlocking a certain ending
- Acting is meh, supporting voice acting is mostly plain bad
- Annoying spelling errors are not always intentional

For examples of similar storytelling that really works: see Oxenfree and Doki Doki Literature Club.

!!!!! THIS REVIEW WILL *NOT* CONTAIN ANY STORY SPOILERS !!!!!

Simulacra is a short single-player experience that takes notes heavily from games such as "Her Story", "Emily is Away", and is eerily similar to "Sara is Missing". Having only played Simulacra, and not having played the others, I wouldn't feel right calling it merely a clone, and so I'll let it stand on its own.

Stemming originally from the point-and-click Adventure Game genres, these new detective-style games seem to be a welcome twist on an old idea. In Simulacra, you play, essentially, yourself. A strange phone has been left on your doorstep, and with seemingly nothing else to do for the day, you find yourself drawn into a mystery that only get stranger as more clues are discovered. 

The masterful design places you in control of the aforementioned phone, and in turn, of eight different phone apps, each more revealing than the last. The apps, meant to mimic modern day social media apps, are your wealth of information, and it shows (as I'm sure the creator intended) exactly how easy it can be to find someone using only a handful of these apps. As the story unravels, it becomes clear that something isn't quite right, and not everyone may be telling the truth. This game was packaged in with a Humble Bundle I purchased, and I was delighted with the experience, which I will outline below.

For a story told through different apps, I found that it (the story) never lost its pacing. As you hope with all good mysteries, I was completely enthralled, and intent on finding out exactly what happened. The lack of soundtrack is made up for with the addition of a host of spooky and scary sounds, ranging from low knocks on a nearby door, to terrifying schreeches from unlocked videos and glitches. This brings me to one of my gripes with the game: the minigame puzzles. 

While the minigames are a welcome break from the plethora of text in the game, I found their solutions to often be sort of convoluted. In fact, the only times that I felt unimmersed were the times I sat, hands on my head, attempting to solve a glorified word jumble, only to find that the answer was often unclear. Similarly, I had a difficult time figuring out the photograph puzzles, in which you stack and unstack layers of corrupted files until you find the ideal stacking formation that removes all corruption. Thankfully, these minigames were few and far in between, and most of my time was spent enjoying the different situations and obstacles in the way of my investigation. Hopping between apps in the game is as effortless as it is in real life, and made for very smooth transitions, and very little downtime as I progressed. 

The characters are pretty solid. It's a rich cast, and I was thankful to hear a notable quality in the performance of the actors. While there were one or two lines which made me cringe, the overall performances were fantastic, which bodes well for any completionists who plan to play multiple runs of this game, in order to live all the different outcomes. The voice acting was mostly really solid, and the video performances followed suit. I honestly could have done without all the spooky whispers and door knocks that were staggered throughout the playthrough. review_text_raw:
The Good Stuff:

The layout and idea behind the game is pretty cool. I like how each "app" generally feels like a real app where you can do whatever, like comment of peoples posts or call random numbers. It is really neat design idea and it is well executed.

I also enjoyed a few of the more difficult puzzles, as they really added a sense of immersion into digging through someone's phone. The puzzles are mainly pretty easy, but the game doesn't baby you through them at all, so you feel smart when you manage to pull of something a bit more complicated.

The Bad Stuff:

For me, story is one of the most important parts of a game like this, and unfortunately SIMULACRA fails to deliver a good one.

Mild Spoilers: [spoiler]While the ending tried to be Black Mirror-esque, I feel like the story fails to properly set up the ending, so it kinda comes out of nowhere. Also, many things in the story aren't well explained or left to Deus Ex Machina[/spoiler]

There are multiple endings, and you will get an idea of what they all are when you finish the game. Some of the potential outcomes have me slightly curious, but not enough to replay it to see them. Perhaps the story would have been more interesting had I gotten a different ending.

I am not a huge fan of horror, but I have played games like Prey and Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice that have a creepy horror feel. The creepiness of SIMULACRA lasts only about the first 30 mins and then you become generally innoculated.

The main title song was also pretty cheesy.

As many other reviews have pointed out, some of the voice acting is on the level of "so bad it's hilarious".

I understand that with a smaller scale game like this it is difficult, but I felt like the chat options often strong-armed me into things I didn't want to say, which made things like [spoiler]gaining Taylor's trust[/spoiler] feel unfair.

The Bottom Line: If you want a game with a good story, there are better games. If you want a game where choices matter, there are better games. If you want a horror game, there are better games. If you just want to see a cool mechanic in action, then you might want to check it out.

review_text_raw:
A fun, innovative experience involving navigating someone’s digital life to find out what happened to someone.

Background: I like playing interactive stories like this while I’m eating instead of watching TV or a movie. It’s good to play these kinds of games between bites.

I didn’t know what to make of this game—I think I got it as part of a bundle—but installed it and tried it out after running through a few movie games and wanting to shift to something else. I was pleasantly surprised by the story, and the gameplay was similar to games like Her Story and Orwell where you interact with a digital interface to make the story unfold.

The Positives:
-It really does feel like you are a person who found a phone and are trying to find out what happened to the owner. There are a few times where it is imperfect in terms of what you probably could/should/would do, but it does a good enough job that it felt realistic enough to suspend disbelief for several hours.

-The phone was fun to play around with—you go into various apps and learn about the owner’s recent activity and then even get to participate a little.

-The people you interact with are sketchy as hell, but it definitely made things interesting.

-The ending got pretty wild; while the horror elements are minimal for most of the game, the ending combines the genres of tech-thrillers and evil-spirit-horror—very interesting. It’s not simply like System Shock 2 or Terminator (where the tech tries to control you) or Evil Dead or The Ring (where evil spirits are trying to kill you); it’s an interesting mix.

-The people involved did a great job—there are a lot of photos, videos, and conversations, and both the actors and the developers did a great job of making it all fit together. It all felt real—I never thought for a moment that the photos or videos were “fake” or “made-for-the-game”. That’s all I look for in acting; not everything has to be Meryl Streep, and this felt real enough.

-The ending was fresh for me—the combination of it being just slightly different from other endings in the genre along with the uniqueness of me having to make decisions that led to the outcome made the experience very new and interesting.

The Negatives:
-As I mentioned, the people you interact with are sketchy, which I overall enjoyed but it does result in some weird interactions. I thought it worked, but I wouldn’t be surprised if you played and said, “Why don’t they just do X?” — I felt that any plot holes were covered up well enough for me to buy it, but you might not.

-If you like a lot of horror, there isn’t much here—it ratchets up near the end but for the most part is more of a mystery with a dash of spooky/thriller elements. I liked the amount, but you might want more.

-It’s tough to strike a balance between elements that build the character and world with ones that begin to give you hints about the mystery…I think they did a good job, but you might find that early on you go through a lot of videos and photos that don’t reveal much. The photos are easy enough to skim through, but you’ll watch several videos and they don’t really do much other than give you a live look at what the owner looked like while slowly introducing the fact that something is amiss. If you’re a narrative critic, you’d probably want them to have done more with those elements than just a look into the life of the owner.

Overall, it’s an interesting game. I was engaged most of the time and there are only brief periods where there is a lot of text back-and-forth that you might want something more to be happening—but it’s not bad by any means. If you are sucked in at those points, you will enjoy it. If not, that’s probably where you might tune out. The good news is that the developers listened and put in the ability to adjust the speed, etc. of the game (especially if you’re replaying it) to solve for that issue. So I think you’ll be okay. As long as you like the mysterious look-into-the-life-of-someone-else genre of point-and-click games (like the “found footage” genre of movies but for video games), you’ll enjoy it. If you are hoping for a lot of horror, though, there isn’t too much and so I just hope to set your expectations appropriately.

The setting is a good idea. They are achieving a good ambiance with background noises that are really well mixed.
This is the only positive point in my experience.

The actual gameplay is very linear and highly undynamic. The investigation part of the game feels more like a checklist then actually trying to understand the persons involved. Why is that? The characters are all very plain and are represented in bad writing. They feel stereotypical to a point were I was only annoyed by their presence and had to figure out how to deal with their stupidity. Their language felt really unnatural and to top it off some video clips and voice calls to top it all off.
There were some interesting ideas, but in general the game feels rushed in really unpolished.
The options of dialogue were pretty straight forward, but as I already said it there are little subbranches to discover. The decision you make are making minor differences in the end scene. The achievements are less of a challenge, more a lure into replaying a game that has little to no replay value.

4€ is a little price, I cant recommend it. If you have the money to spare I recommend games on Steam that are driven by passionate teams that are putting an continuous effort into improving their games. I highly recommend Terraria that is often available for 5€ on sale.

Simulacra, developed by Kaigan Games OÜ and published by Kaigan Games OÜ alongside Neon Doctrine, is a gripping and unnerving found-phone horror game that masterfully blends storytelling, mystery, and interactive gameplay. The game places players in the shoes of a person who discovers a lost phone belonging to a woman named Anna, who has mysteriously disappeared. This innovative format taps into contemporary fears about technology and privacy, creating a tense and intimate atmosphere that keeps players hooked from start to finish.

Such a creative horror game!
A phone is left on your doorstep. Like the kind stranger you are, you unlock it to start looking for the owner, but it becomes obvious really quickly that something is wrong...

This game is great because it hooks you right from the start, but it has some flaws. The good things first: The story is very interesting. The entire mystery of where anna is and why the phone is doing the stuff its doing is captivating. Having to puzzle together stuff like passwords from info on the phone is fun, and the athmosphere when playing with headphones is also great, the ambience noises like knocking or someone breathing down your neck all of a sudden sound so realistic It starteled me a few times. Multipe endings also give it replayability.

Now the bad. While for the most part the game does not rely on jumpscares it has some. Not the worst thing, but it jumpscares feel cheap compared to the rest of the atmosphere. The acting. Idk if it was supposed to feel so campy, but it really did (an exeption here would be [spoiler] the simulacra. I really enjoyed the voice acting for it [/spoiler]. This is fine for the most part, you basically work with them for the greater good to find Anna, but what kind of pissed me off was that you [spoiler] HAVE to be nice to Taylor and trust him to unlock the only good ending. This guy is NOT trustworthy [/spoiler]

Still had a BLAST with it and would reccomend playing it!

review_text_raw:
[This review made after getting two bad endings out of 5 possible endings]

I like this game and I would recommend it, first and foremost, to players that are interested in STORY or, at least, world 
building. The game is not difficult: picture puzzles, word arranging, and some light fact searching comprise the bulk of the challenges. The meat of the game is in the dialogue choices, and this is where the replayability come from. You don't really get locked out of most options when taking/talking different ways, so you can express your moral flexibility without fearing that you'll reach a dead-end. As for content, they did a decent job of fleshing out with stuff that makes it feel like a "lived with" phone. The game does a good job of simulating smartphone usage with the apps, pics and their poses, vids, and social media content. A nice touch, is that there is a checklist of tasks that would help the truly clueless and serve as a guide for those looking for certain keystone events to play around with on subsequent playthroughs. This checklist is out of the way though for those who don't want hints on what to do next.


On the negative side, some of the voice acting, for me, was off if not "unsuitable". The delivery of the voice only lines truly felt and sounded "rehearsed". The VOs not sounding natural kind of sticks out like a sore thumb amid the aptness of the pictures and videos to a phone setting. The worst offender of this, sorry to say to the voice actor, is the Greg character. Truly, to me, it sounded like he was voicing a cartoon character instead of making a call, and it kind of took me out of the general mood of the game.

I think, the ending, will be pretty hit or miss for some people as well. I want to liken how the ending progresses to one of the scenes in a movie, but that would probably spoil it a bit. It's just that most people that saw it back then went "Wait what was that again?" Don't get me wrong, I'm fine with the endings I got (two bad endings), but the way to the climax was tedious, especially since I don't know if there is a message skip button for when you are doing a replay and you know what is going to be said. A note on the endings I got, it seems like you get locked to a set of outcomes after some threshold. I know my choices at the end didn't end up changing any of my final options. 

All in all, a decent casual horror sim game with some replayability, a fleshed out setting, hit or miss voice acting, and an endgame sequence (not ending, the stuff leading up to the ending) that'll make you go "excuse you? whowherewhenhowwhywhatnow?". 

For now, at full price, it would depend on your affinity for games like these to buy it for around a 5 hour single playthrough (worth it if you go with the $1 per hour of gameplay mindset). It is a decent recommend to buy if it ever has a sale at some point though.

It's good but you need to be able to look past 4 big faults to really get into it, as the game can kinda work on moon logic sometimes and it sets you up for failure, not to mention a few other plot holes. 

Also the story is completely railroaded, it has multiple endings but no matter which ending you're going to get, the story and game is pretty much the exact same aside from VERY MINOR character dialog and Ashley not talking to you depending on your choices, until the final scene where it will use choices you made in the past and whether or not you do a specific thing right before the final scene, to determine if Anna and Taylor, the two main characters, are destined to die, or if not, whether or not only one of them will live or if both of them are going to live.

It only branches out and stops being railroaded in the climax and resolution of the game, and since it outright encourages you to replay it to get all the endings, it can't really get away with assuming that people will only play it once, especially since it's extremely easy to fall into the worst ending if you don't do everything right.

Outside of these things, and if you can get past it, this game is good and fun, an intriguing concept and I like Taylor even if he's a total dork. But don't play the phone version as the loops in audio are not as smooth as on the PC version and I experienced a bug that ruined every FMV in the final scene, so you should get it on steam for PC like here.

review_text_raw:
Okay, so i just finished playing this (took me something like 5 or 6 hours I believe), and I felt compelled to review this game because it's like nothing I've played before. I had never heard of the "found-phone" genre in games before.

First let me say this: if you're a fan of mysteries, riddles, horror, or to be more specific, found-footage horror, then this game is for you! If not, try it anyway lol you just might be surprised.

This game starts out with you booting up a phone that was sent to you (or left on your doorstep, it's not totally cleared up in the story), and when you do it begins to glitch out a little and then these texts start coming in, and well, it just takes off from there...

The basic premise is that the owner of the phone, a girl named Anna, has gone missing and it's up to you (and a couple others along the way) to try to find her. You do this by digging through her phone and reading EVERYTHING, and then communicating with some of her contacts through texts and emails and an online dating app and a twitter-like app.  As things progress you learn that she has dissapeared and it may be connected to other recent dissapearances (but I won't go into more on that because I don't want to ruin the experience for new players).  Eventually, you realize there's a lot more going on than meets the eye.

The game has a very unnerving, intense feeling to it, and is all the better for it.  It has a decent story, some fun little mini games and riddles, a good amount of investigation and some pretty convinging dialogues, and for the REALLY hardcore sleuths out there, it even has some very interesting "easter eggs" hidden in the game that are quite rewarding to find. (I'll give you a hint here, but that's it...morse code, click it :)   )

As for graphics, sound, story, gameplay, etc...well graphics aren't important here as it's basically a phone emulator, the gameplay is as simple as digging through a phone and talking to people and looking stuff up (but you need a brain lol), the story is interesting enough that you really will never get bored in a single playthrough, and apparently it has many different endings so it has replayability there...where this game really shines though is the sound...it's incredible and really really well done.  When you start they recommend you use headphones, and I STRONGLY recommend you take their advice, it's just not the same on speakers, not even close

Anyway, the TL;DR is this:
if you 're looking for an action title, look elsewhere, but if you're looking for an EXPERIENCE that really makes you feel like you're a part of a mystery that needs to be solved, I can't recommend this highly enough. It's fun as hell!

For me it's a 4.5/5

My first experience with the found phone game genre was disappointing. I found [I]Replica[/I] to be an undercooked, preachy, borderline sciolistic game that is best not played. My excitement for this genre was quashed quickly, but I remembered that I still have [I]SIMULACRA[/I] in my backlog of games. Because of that, I decided to give found phone games another try.

Coincidentally, [I]SIMULACRA[/I] was partly inspired by [I]Replica[/I] (as seen by the titles), and partly by [I]Her Story[/I], one of my favourite games of all time. I loved [I]Her Story[/I] for its intriguing narrative and presentation, so I had some hope for [I]SIMULACRA[/I]. Thankfully, after my disheartening first exposure to found phone games, [I]SIMULACRA[/I] did not disappoint.

[I]SIMULACRA[/I] is a mystery game, in which you find a phone that belongs to a woman named Anna. By digging deep into her personal life chronicled by the contents of her phone and Internet activities, you uncover clues as to why Anna had gone missing. The puzzles in this game are fun, fair, and hardly difficult. Because of that, the game manages to present the story in a nice flow. It also helps that [I]SIMULACRA[/I] has a slick presentation, with a clean, Android-like user interface that controls well with mouse and keyboard. The in-game videos are pretty well done, too, but I did find the voice acting for one particular character to be laughable.

Despite [I]SIMULACRA[/I] being described or classified as a horror game, I did not find it scary.  Aside from a few instances, in which some players may find the game's version of a "jump scare" frightening, I considered this game to be more suspenseful. You can feel the plot thickening and tension building as the game progresses, with some subtle (but usually not so subtle) graphical and audio alterations making the game increasingly unnerving. The way [I]SIMULACRA[/I]'s story unfolds is almost Hitchcockian.

As much as I enjoyed the game narrative, I did find the ending slightly abrupt. It seemed like there is more story to tell, and perhaps the spin-off game, [I]SIMULACRA: Pipe Dreams[/I], may tie up some loose ends. Still, [I]SIMULACRA[/I] is a very enjoyable game, made even better if played in the dark with earphones on. The developers smartly included a "Begin+" mode that will unlock after the first playthrough. This mode allows you to replay the entire game with sped-up text, so you can retry certain scenarios without needing to sit through the slow, deliberate pace of the chat sessions. (It's also a time saver for achievement hunters.) [I]SIMULACRA[/I] gets an enthusiastic recommendation from me.

P.S.: I wrote this review after completing [I]Sara is Missing[/i] the predecessor of this game. [I]SIMULACRA[/I] shares many similarities with [I]S.I.M.[/I] (Coincidence? review_text_raw:
Love this game. In the same vein as films like 'Searching', you spend all of your time navigating a device (in this case a phone) in search of a missing person. Simulacra has more a horror tone than 'Searching', but for much of the game's runtime it's only lightly scary, with most of the suspense coming not from supernatural frights but from further unraveling the mystery by feeling like an amateur cybersleuth. 

There are definitely moments where it was frustrating trying to figure out where to go next, but the game generally does a good job of pointing you in the right direction through the use of hints given by the characters in the game. It all feels organic and never too forced. Multiple playthroughs will be needed to see all of the endings, but even just one playthrough will give every player a satisfying experience in the end. 

My few gripes with this game are that the actors aren't really that great in their performances, and for a game that I think is set in the US (at least that seems like the accent everyone is going for), the actor's accents waver quite often. This is obviously not a big budget production, so it's understandable that top shelf talent isn't within reach, but I would say that instead of trying to force a setting, just go with what's available around you. I don't feel that the US setting is necessary to tell this kind of story. I'd also like if there were some way to expedite replays of the game. Yes, if you do a second playthrough you can skip text much more quickly, but I'm thinking of something kinda like Zero Escape: Virtue's Last Reward. In that title there was a branching path menu you could pull up and jump exactly to the point where the story diverged. That would save so much time replaying up until the point where a critical decision was made. 

Conclusion:

Fun cyberdetective game told through a smartphone. Elements of horror, but nothing too overdone so that non-horror fans couldn't enjoy. Gameplay makes you do a fair amount of thinking, without too much handholding, so you feel a sense of accomplishment when you unearth another clue. Tons of easter eggs are there for those willing to look. Performances are not great here, but the voiced parts are minimal and don't interrupt the flow too often.

review_text_raw:
Having played "A Normal Lost Phone", the concept of Simulacra isn't anything new to me, however due to this not being a particularly common way of making a game it is a welcome addition to this genre of sorts. 
Simulacra also comes with a couple of different twists compared to what "A Normal Lost Phone" had so it's not complete copy.

The good:
*You are thrown into an interesting story that you have to go through with the help of strangers. Who should you trust? Who should you be weary of? Wel that's the beauty, you don't know and you have to base your judgements on scraps of information that you can find. The story is definitely one of the highlights of this game.
*The gameplay whilst isn't groundbreaking works well for this game and doesn't propose any friction for the player on how to proceed.
*There's a decent bit of replayability in this game if you want to uncover all of the different paths. They also aren't particularly difficult to reach if given enough thought.

The bad:
*The horror elements of this game... Don't get me wrong, I love myself some horror and this game seems like a good candidate for a bit of it, however the way it is implemented in this specific game is forced and cliche.
Build tension through uneasiness, not through awful jumpscares.
*I don't need to be redirected to a webpage with a Discord server every time I finish the game. It is annoying. If I want to join your Discord Ill find a way to do it without it being showed in my face every time.
*For a game with so many branching I feel like it should've had a save system. If you want to get a specific achievement you are forced to replay the whole game. It is remedied by the faster conversations, but I do not want to listen to the same conversation for 7 times just so I can get an achievement.
*The acting leaves some things to be desired. I understand that this is an indie game but the video segments in this game felt somewhat robotic and lifeless.

Overall, Simulacra is a fun and interesting little game, that will not burn a hole in your wallet and will keep you entertained for a day or two. I think its worth giving a try, if you can stand the occasional jumpscare.

review_text_raw:
[i]Simulacra[/i] is a captivating puzzle-slash-detective-slash-horror-slash-social commentary game which is yours to enjoy for a delightfully economic entree fee.

So you found a phone on your doorstep and it appears to belong to the now missing twenty-something Anna. Your quest to find out what happened to her will take place entirely through the smartphone interface, trying to get into contact with her familiars, sifting through her social media posts and recovering lost files. Soon enough the mysteries start to pile up. Those who have a basic grasp of the philosophy of Jean Baudrillard may already guess what's behind the sudden disappearance.

It's a short game which will take approximately 4-5 hours to finish, which is enough to get involved with the characters while still short enough so that the gameplay does not grow stale. There is replay value to be had, since your decisions (who to trust, what to do) can take the story to different conclusions.

The game touches on a few social issues, such as [spoiler]sexual harassment[/spoiler], [spoiler]the banality of social media content[/spoiler] and [spoiler]the ongoing digitization of society[/spoiler], but I never found the game to be either too preachy or too political. There is also some existential philosophy woven into the dialogues, though it's enough to give you something to muse about, it's too little to be considered profound. The puzzles are fairly easy, making the game more appealing to casual gamers rather than seasoned point-and-click fanatics.

At the bottom of all its qualities are certainly the jump scares. While it can be argued that this much loathed trope does the trick (i.e.: keeping you on edge even during the quiet moments), they are still a cheap substitute for the subtleties of psychological horror. That said, the game did manage to frighten me through the sheer eeriness of a digital device continually distorting into absolute madness, but the rather bland acting in the audio/video files often pulled me out of suspense-belief and back into the comfort zone.

[b][u]Final verdict:[/u] 7/10[/b]. [i]Simulacra[/i] is a fresh and well-executed, though somewhat poorly acted missing person mystery.

[h1]👍 Highly Recommended[/h1]

[i]SIMULACRA is one of the few games that genuinely makes browsing through a smartphone feel fun. It's a horror game of sorts, but Instead of running from monsters or hiding in closets, you're piecing together the disappearance of a young woman by exploring every corner of her phone. Messages, photos, videos, emails, social media, and browser history slowly reveal a mystery that's equal parts psychological thriller and supernatural horror. It feels disturbingly believable-almost like scrolling through someone else's real device.[/i]
[hr][/hr]
[h2]🟢 PROS[/h2]
[list]
[*][b]Brilliant Found Phone Concept:[/b] Investigating an entire mystery through a lost smartphone is an incredibly immersive idea that still feels unique years after release.
[*][b]Excellent Storytelling:[/b] The narrative unfolds naturally through text messages, emails, videos, and social media instead of lengthy exposition. Every app contains another piece of the puzzle.
[*][b]Convincing Characters:[/b] Conversations feel surprisingly authentic. Friends, coworkers, and family all have believable personalities and motivations, making the investigation feel personal.
[*][b]Genuinely Creepy:[/b] SIMULACRA builds tension through unsettling discoveries, disturbing videos, and the feeling that something is deeply wrong with the phone itself.
[*][b]Creative Puzzles:[/b] Unlocking files, recovering deleted data, solving passwords, and navigating fake apps keeps the gameplay engaging throughout.
[*][b]Multiple Endings:[/b] Your decisions matter, giving the story additional replay value.
[/list]
[hr][/hr]
[h2]🔴 CONS[/h2]
[list]
[*][b]Live-Action Acting Can Be Uneven:[/b] Most performances are convincing, but a handful of scenes feel slightly awkward compared to the otherwise strong production.
[*][b]Occasional Interface Frustrations:[/b] Searching through apps or revisiting conversations can sometimes be more cumbersome than necessary.
[*][b]The Ending May Divide Players:[/b] Without spoilers, the final revelations won't satisfy everyone, especially those hoping for a more grounded explanation.
[/list]
[hr][/hr]
[h2]💰 VALUE FOR MONEY[/h2]
[b]Excellent[/b] — SIMULACRA offers several hours of engaging investigation packed with memorable moments, clever puzzles, and one of the most original horror concepts in the genre. It's frequently discounted on Steam, making it an even easier recommendation for fans of narrative adventures and psychological horror.
[hr][/hr]
[h3]⭐ 9/10[/h3]
[i]A brilliantly executed smartphone horror that proves the scariest place in a horror game isn't an abandoned mansion. Immersive, unsettling, and remarkably original, SIMULACRA remains one of the most engaging narrative horror experiences available on Steam.[/i]

review_text_raw:
I am generally biased to be forgiving of FMV interactive movies, so of course I've played others like Her Story, #WarGames, The Bunker, Late Shift, and The Shapeshifting Detective.  Like those games, this game is relatively short on total content, with moments of good acting and then...well, near-miss moments that make you cringe.  Also, these games tend to have multiple achievements and scenes that you can't get in one playthrough, which is a way of extending the replay value, but I seldom feel particularly inclined to watch the repeated parts over and over again.

This game is unique due to the phone interface and the clever design that it took to make that work.  You feel like it really could be you deciding what to do in this situation, but then sometimes you're reminded how you can't actually do anything like answer a phone call.  So when it works, it's great, but it has built-in limitations to just how far the concept can go.  I commend them for the creepy story.  I wish the really uneven voice acting hadn't pulled me out of it from time to time.  At least Anna (whose phone you've found) is done consistently well.

Your first full playthrough will take 3-4 hours depending on how much you read, and subsequent plays should take you a bit less.  Alternate achievements, videos, conversations, and endings are basically earned by the responses you choose, like who to be nice to, who to scold, and who to trust.  The downside of that is like the decisions in Telltale games, especially The Walking Dead: you'll have to replay with lots of choices that you'd never make in real life if you want to see the other paths.  In that regard, replays are more like gaming the game and less like experiencing the story.  But overall, that's a complaint that's bound to be true of every choose-your-own-adventure game you can find.  So you know what you're getting.  If you like that, and you have a tolerance for FMV games, this one is certainly worth $5.

review_text_raw:
A decent enough experience!
The story revolves around the player who receives a phone by a missing girl by the name of Anna and you  must figure out where she went missing and save her while also figuring out about what is causing the many disappearances that have been happening on a dating app. The characters in this game are really cringy and can be hard to enjoy or even have a connection with. The story itself is alright as it does help carry the game along, but its nothing special. 
There really isn't a setting as it takes place all on a phone but its a pretty unique scenario for the player to be put in. 
The visuals are fine as it is all just meant to be a smart phone, but it does look really clean and is convincing enough to feel like a smart phone. 
Sound and audio are again fine as there is really only one bit of soundtrack when opening the game which is a pretty nice piece. The audio is a hit and miss as the audio that is used when the player makes interactions with the phone are good but the background noise that is meant to scare the player does a really poor job at that as it will get to a point where the player would have heard them enough to have no reaction towards it which is disappointing.
The gameplay is fairly simple as all you do is either select different dialog choices, do mini puzzles to load back information and finding clues to move on in the story. Gameplay is decent enough as the story that it intertwines with help it feel more satisfying to do. Finally, i do like the fact that there are multiple endings and outcomes that you experience through the game which would give it more replay-ability
Overall, Simulacra does has a few flaws but if you looking for a decent, unique experience to kill a few hours with i would definitely recommend this.
